say.text: Two outlet problems can look alike at the bedside.
Patient A is a 71-year-old woman with three days of vomiting, epigastric fullness and weight loss. Endoscopy shows a gallstone wedged in her duodenum.
Which diagnosis fits patient A?

choices.label: Gallstone ileus, stone in the duodenum
Bouveret's syndrome, stone in the duodenum
Gallstone ileus, stone at the pylorus
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. A gallstone impacted in the duodenum or pylorus causes gastric outlet obstruction, which is Bouveret's syndrome.
That choice is not right.

Ileus sounds like the word for any stone that obstructs, so it tempts you. But gallstone ileus is a small-bowel obstruction from a stone that has passed through a fistula. A stone held in the duodenum blocks the stomach outlet.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so read the symptoms: vomiting with epigastric fullness is the stomach failing to empty, which is the outlet picture and not a lower bowel one.

say.text: That choice is not right.
The pylorus is an outlet site, so you were close, but the name is wrong. A stone that causes ileus has already moved on and lodges further down, most often in the terminal ileum.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so tie the name to the site: stone at the outlet is Bouveret's, stone in the terminal ileum is gallstone ileus.

say.text: Ask which part of the gut the stone has blocked: the outlet from the stomach, or the lower small bowel.

Bouveret's syndrome is gastric outlet obstruction from a gallstone impacted in the duodenum or pylorus. Gallstone ileus is a different picture, a stone that has passed through a fistula and blocks the small bowel.
Patient B is a 74-year-old woman with colicky central pain, vomiting and a small-bowel obstruction. Her abdominal film shows air in the biliary tree and a calcified stone in the lower abdomen.
Which diagnosis, and where is the stone lodged?

choices.label: Bouveret's syndrome, stone in the duodenum
Gallstone ileus, stone in the terminal ileum
Mirizzi syndrome, fistula into the bile duct
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Pneumobilia, small-bowel obstruction and an ectopic stone make Rigler's triad, and the stone most often lodges in the terminal ileum.
That choice is not right.

Both are gallstones in the gut, so Bouveret's tempts you. But it blocks the stomach outlet. Here the obstruction is in the small bowel, with air in the biliary tree and a stone far below in the abdomen.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check where the stone ended up: on her film it lies in the lower abdomen, well past the duodenum.

say.text: That choice is not right.

A fistula features in Mirizzi syndrome too, so the word tempts you. But Mirizzi gives jaundice from a stone pressing on the hepatic duct. This patient has a bowel obstruction and a stone in the lower abdomen, with no jaundice.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so compare the two fistulas: in Mirizzi it joins the gallbladder to the bile duct, while here the fistula let the stone reach the bowel.

say.text: Two clues sit together: the air in the biliary tree and the level of the bowel obstruction. Which single diagnosis explains both?

Gallstone ileus: a large stone passes through a cholecystoenteric fistula and blocks the small bowel, most often in the terminal ileum. Air in the biliary tree with a bowel obstruction and an ectopic stone is Rigler's triad.
A 60-year-old man has jaundice. Ultrasound shows a stone in his gallbladder neck, and cholangiography shows his common hepatic duct narrowed.
What is causing his jaundice?

choices.label: A stone passed into the common bile duct, blocking its lumen
A stone in Hartmann's pouch pressing on the hepatic duct
A stone impacted at the ampulla, blocking the duct
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The stone presses on the common hepatic duct from outside, which is Mirizzi syndrome.
That choice is not right.
A stone in the duct does cause jaundice, so it tempts you. But the scan puts the stone in the gallbladder neck, outside the duct, and the hepatic duct is narrowed from outside.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what the narrowing means: a duct narrowed with the stone sitting beside it is compression, not a stone in the lumen.

say.text: That choice is not right.
The ampulla is the classic place for a jaundice-causing stone, so it tempts you. But this stone sits in the gallbladder neck, and it is the common hepatic duct, higher up, that is narrowed.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so use the geography: the ampulla is the lower end of the duct, whereas Hartmann's pouch lies against the hepatic duct higher up.

say.text: Follow the stone. Ask what it is touching, not what it is sitting inside.
Mirizzi syndrome: a stone in Hartmann's pouch or the cystic duct compresses the common hepatic duct from outside and causes obstructive jaundice. It can erode into a cholecystocholedochal fistula.
Two patients with cholangitis, side by side. Patient C has fever with rigors, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain.
Patient D has all of those, plus low blood pressure and confusion.
What is patient D's named syndrome?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Charcot's triad with hypotension and confusion added is Reynolds' pentad.
That choice is not right. The triad is only the local picture, and the two systemic additions move the case to a different named set.

Charcot's triad is fever with rigors, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. Adding hypotension and confusion gives Reynolds' pentad.
Which set of findings is Charcot's triad in acute cholangitis?

choices.label: Fever, RUQ pain, hypotension and rigors
Fever with rigors, jaundice and RUQ pain
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. The triad is fever with rigors, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain; the pentad adds two more.
That choice is not right. The triad is built from local signs plus fever; hypotension belongs to the extended set.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one deserves a second look. But the triad is built from local signs plus fever; hypotension belongs to the extended set.

say.text: That choice is not right. Hypotension and confusion are the add-ons that make the pentad; they do not form the core set.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one deserves a second look. But hypotension and confusion are the add-ons that make the pentad; they do not form the core set.

say.text: Start with the pain and the skin colour, then ask which systemic sign is in the classic three.
Charcot's triad: fever with rigors, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. Reynolds' pentad adds hypotension and confusion.
A plain film shows gas in the gallbladder wall of an elderly diabetic man.
Which organism is most likely?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Gas-forming infection of the gallbladder, classically in elderly diabetic men, is caused by Clostridium perfringens.
That choice is not right. Gas in the wall points to a gas-forming organism, so the commonest organism in infected bile does not answer this.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one deserves a second look. But gas in the wall points to a gas-forming organism, so the commonest organism in infected bile does not answer this.

say.text: That choice is not right. It is not the classic gas-former for this picture, and treating every infected gallbladder alike is the trap.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one deserves a second look. But it is not the classic gas-former for this picture, and treating every infected gallbladder alike is the trap.

say.text: The gas tells you something about the organism. Which of these is a classic gas-former?

Emphysematous cholecystitis is infection with gas-forming organisms, most often Clostridium perfringens, classically in elderly diabetic men. E. coli is the commonest organism in infected bile in general.
An elderly diabetic man with a septic picture has gas in the gallbladder wall on CT.
What is the right urgency?

choices.label: Antibiotics now, interval surgery in 6-8 weeks
Urgent cholecystectomy or drainage, with antibiotics
Treat as an ordinary infected gallbladder, as E. coli causes both
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Emphysematous cholecystitis carries a high risk of gangrene and perforation, so it needs urgent cholecystectomy or drainage and antibiotics.
That choice is not right.
Waiting for the inflammation to settle is the older plan and feels safe. But gas-forming infection can progress to gangrene and perforation, so it cannot wait weeks.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what the gas means: it signals a gas-forming infection that can perforate, which an interval plan does not protect against.

say.text: That choice is not right.
A routine infected gallbladder is the usual picture, so it tempts you. But gas in the wall means a gas-forming organism, most often Clostridium perfringens, and the urgency is higher.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two pictures: E. coli is the commonest organism in ordinary infected bile, whereas gas points to Clostridium.

say.text: Gas in the wall is a warning sign. Think about what the gas-forming infection can do to the wall, and how quickly.
Emphysematous cholecystitis needs urgent cholecystectomy or drainage with antibiotics, because the risk of gangrene and perforation is high. Delaying for weeks is the wrong model.
Bacteria in infected bile make an enzyme, beta-glucuronidase, that frees bilirubin for stone formation.
Which stone forms from that bile, and where?

choices.label: Brown pigment stones, formed in the bile ducts
Black pigment stones, formed in the gallbladder
Black pigment stones, formed in the bile ducts
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Brown pigment stones are soft and earthy, form in the bile ducts, and follow infection and stasis.
That choice is not right. Black stones are linked to chronic haemolysis and cirrhosis, not to infected bile.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one deserves a second look. But black stones are linked to chronic haemolysis and cirrhosis, not to infected bile.

say.text: That choice is not right. The cause in this stem is infection, and infection goes with the other pigment stone, not with black.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this one deserves a second look. But the cause in this stem is infection, and infection goes with the other pigment stone, not with black.

say.text: Match the cause first. Which pigment stone is linked to infection, and which to haemolysis?

Brown pigment stones form in the bile ducts with biliary infection and stasis; bacterial beta-glucuronidase frees bilirubin for them. Black pigment stones form in the gallbladder with chronic haemolysis or cirrhosis.
A student's note reads, 'A palpable gallbladder in a jaundiced patient means carcinoma of the head of the pancreas.'
Which correction makes the note right?

choices.label: Drop 'jaundiced': any palpable gallbladder means cancer
Add 'tender': a tender palpable gallbladder in jaundice means cancer
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. In a jaundiced patient, a palpable non-tender gallbladder suggests malignant distal obstruction rather than stones.
That choice is not right. Dropping 'jaundiced' removes the qualifier that makes the rule apply, because the rule concerns a palpable gallbladder with jaundice.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this deserves a second look. The rule only applies when the patient is jaundiced.

say.text: That choice is not right.
Tenderness points to an inflamed gallbladder, as in cholecystitis, empyema or mucocele, so the rule needs a non-tender gallbladder. A tender one does not suggest malignant obstruction.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so reverse the qualifier: the law is about a jaundiced patient with a gallbladder that is palpable and not tender.

say.text: Which finding must be present before the law applies at all?

Courvoisier's law: in a jaundiced patient, a palpable non-tender gallbladder is unlikely to be due to stones and suggests malignant distal obstruction. A tender gallbladder without jaundice, as in empyema or mucocele, does not contradict it.
A 58-year-old man with diabetes has gallstones found incidentally on ultrasound. He has never had pain.
Which statement about operating is right?

choices.label: Observe; older PYQ keys listed diabetes as an indication
Operate now, since stones in a diabetic always cause complications
Operate now, since gallstones raise the risk of gallbladder cancer
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Asymptomatic stones are generally observed, with roughly 1-2% a year developing symptoms. Older PYQ keys listed diabetes as an indication, but current practice does not routinely advise it.
That choice is not right.
Diabetes does make complications feel likely, so it tempts you. But most stones stay silent, and current practice does not routinely remove them in diabetes. Older PYQ keys did list it.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so keep both columns: older key says diabetes is an indication, current practice observes asymptomatic stones.

say.text: That choice is not right.

Gallbladder cancer is a real concern, so it tempts you. But gallstones alone do not justify surgery; prophylactic removal is for high-risk features such as porcelain gallbladder, stones over 3 cm or polyps over 1 cm.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so name the real indications: porcelain gallbladder, stones over 3 cm, polyp over 1 cm, sickle cell disease.

say.text: Ask two questions: does he have symptoms, and does current practice treat diabetes alone as a reason to operate?

Asymptomatic stones need no treatment in most patients, and only about 1-2% a year become symptomatic. Prophylactic surgery is for selected high-risk cases. Older PYQ keys listed diabetes, so learn both.
A man with gallstones is admitted with acute pancreatitis. His registrar asks about the commonest cause of acute pancreatitis overall.
Which answer is right?

choices.label: Gallstones and alcohol are equally common
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. Gallstones are the commonest cause of acute pancreatitis, followed by alcohol, so a gallstone patient with pancreatitis is the classic picture.
That choice is not right. Alcohol is the second cause, with gallstones the commonest.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this deserves a second look. Alcohol is the famous cause, but the ranking puts gallstones first.

say.text: That choice is not right. The two are ranked: gallstones are the commonest cause, followed by alcohol.

say.text: Think of the stone disease you have just studied. Where does it rank among causes of acute pancreatitis?
Gallstones are the commonest cause of acute (gallstone) pancreatitis, followed by alcohol. It is one of the complications of gallstone disease.
